title: Comet ATLAS shattered into fragments near the Sun: how thermal stress destroyed it and why icy cores collapse
byline: Сollin Rugg View all posts by Сollin Rugg
excerpt: Wondering why comet ATLAS broke apart? Discover the mechanics of outgassing, solar heating, and rotational spin-up that cause fragile cosmic iceballs to disintegrate.
content:
Comet ATLAS disintegrated because intense solar radiation vaporised subsurface volatile ice, generating violent gas jets that spun its fragile nucleus until structural stresses tore it to shreds. As the celestial body swept closer to the Sun, rising temperatures triggered relentless outgassing, turning a porous mix of dust, frozen water, and organic gravel into a disintegrating cloud of cosmic rubble.

Astronomers and stargazers across Britain had tracked the incoming object with great anticipation, hoping for a dazzling naked-eye spectacle across clear night skies. Instead, telescope images revealed multiple fractured pieces where a unified nucleus had once been, cutting the show short and leaving casual observers wondering why did comet atlas break apart before reaching its brightest potential.

The Physics of Destruction: How Solar Radiation Shatters Comets

Comets are not monolithic boulders of solid stone; rather, they are loosely aggregated “dirty snowballs” composed of frozen gases, silicates, and carbonaceous grains left behind from the formation of our solar system. Held together by remarkably weak gravitational forces and delicate molecular cohesion, their internal integrity remains precarious at best.

When such an object journeys from the frigid outskirts of deep space towards perihelion—its closest approach to the Sun—the sudden spike in thermal energy induces acute thermal shock. Volatiles such as frozen carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, and water ice do not melt into liquid form in the vacuum of space. Instead, they sublimate instantly into expanding gas, creating substantial subterranean pressure cavities.

WARNING: THIS WILL CHANGE EVERYTHING!

The structural collapse of an incoming comet is rarely a single event; it is an escalating chain reaction triggered when internal gas pressures overcome the minimal tensile strength of primordial ice.

As these pockets of gas rupture through the crust, they erupt into the vacuum as powerful asymmetric jets. These outgassing vents act precisely like miniature rocket thrusters firing uncontrollably across the surface of the nucleus.

The Lethal Role of Rotational Spin-up

If these natural thrusters fire unevenly across irregular topography, they impart angular momentum to the comet, causing it to spin faster and faster on its axis. This runaway phenomenon is widely recognised by astrophysicists as rotational disruption.

  • Asymmetric outgassing: Non-uniform venting pushes the uneven nucleus off-kilter.
  • Critical spin rate: Centrifugal force increases at the outer edges of the body until it exceeds the comet’s fragile self-gravity.
  • Structural fission: The core develops deep fissures, fracturing cleanly or crumbling along pre-existing fault lines.

Once fission begins, exposed fresh ice from the interior faces direct sunlight for the first time, sparking immediate, explosive bursts of sublimation that blow smaller pieces further apart.

Fragile Composition: Monolith or Cosmic Rubble Pile?

A widespread misconception among the public is that comets break up because they suffer high-velocity collisions with rogue space rocks or drift too close to the atmosphere. In truth, destruction almost always comes from within, dictated entirely by physical density and porosity.

Property Typical Cometary Nucleus Characteristics
Structural Integrity Porous rubble pile bound by minimal gravity
Primary Volatiles Frozen water, carbon monoxide, and methane
Primary Disruption Triggers Sublimation pressure and rapid rotational spin-up
Visual Consequence Sudden temporary brightening followed by fading

When internal fracture occurs, the overall surface area exposed to solar radiation increases exponentially within hours. This sudden expansion creates a temporary, deceptive spike in brightness as a massive volume of liberated dust catches the sunlight, closely preceding total dissipation into an invisible trail of debris.

Astronomers relying on ground telescopes and space observatories like SOHO frequently witness cometary bodies shedding material before disintegrating altogether. The fate of ATLAS highlights the persistent unpredictability of pristine Oort Cloud visitors making their first journey into intense inner-system heat.
